title: The 50/30/20 Budget Explained Simply (With a Real Example)

scenes.heading: Where Did Your Paycheck Go?
lines: You get paid, and two weeks later the money is just gone, and you're not sure where it went.
One simple rule can fix that: fifty, thirty, twenty.
By the end, you'll know your own three numbers, down to the dollar.

scenes.heading: What Is the 50/30/20 Rule?
lines: The idea is simple. You split your take-home pay into three buckets.
Fifty percent goes to needs, the things you must pay to live and work.
Thirty percent goes to wants, the fun stuff that makes life enjoyable.
And twenty percent goes to your future: savings and paying down debt.
It was made popular by Elizabeth Warren and her daughter, Amelia, in their book All Your Worth.

scenes.heading: Step 1: Find Your Take-Home Pay
lines: Step one: start with your take-home pay, not your salary.
That's what actually lands in your bank account after taxes.
If money for retirement comes out of your paycheck, count it toward your twenty percent.
Let's use an example: three thousand dollars a month.

scenes.heading: Step 2: Do the Math
lines: With three thousand dollars, the math is quick.
Fifteen hundred dollars for needs.
Nine hundred dollars for wants.
And six hundred dollars for savings and extra debt payments.
That's it. Three numbers, and every dollar has a job.

scenes.heading: The 50%: Needs
lines: Needs are the bills you'd still have to pay, even in a hard month.
Rent or mortgage, utilities, and basic groceries.
Getting to work, like a car payment, gas, or a bus pass.
Insurance, child care, and the minimum payment on every debt.
Notice: groceries are a need, but takeout is not.

scenes.heading: The 30%: Wants
lines: Wants are everything that's nice to have, but not required.
Eating out, streaming services, new clothes, and hobbies.
Trips, concerts, and that upgrade to the newest phone.
And here's the part people love: this money is meant to be spent, guilt free.
A budget you actually enjoy is a budget you'll actually stick to.

scenes.heading: The 20%: Your Future
lines: The last twenty percent is for future you.
First, build a small emergency fund, so surprises don't turn into new debt.
Next, pay extra on high-interest debt, like credit cards.
Then save for retirement and your bigger goals.
Remember, minimum payments count as needs. Anything extra you pay goes here.

scenes.heading: Step 3: Check Your Real Numbers
lines: Now the eye-opening part: compare the plan with what you really spend.
Pull up your last two or three months of bank and card statements.
Sort each purchase into needs, wants, or savings.
Most people are surprised. Wants often hide in small, everyday charges.

scenes.heading: What If Needs Are Over 50%?
lines: Here's the question people ask most: what if my needs take way more than half?
That's really common, especially with high rent or a low income.
It doesn't mean you failed. The numbers are a target, not a law.
Try sixty, twenty, twenty for a while, or even seventy, twenty, ten.
The one thing to protect is saving something, even if it's small.

scenes.heading: Shrink Your Needs Over Time
lines: Then chip away at your needs, bit by bit.
Shop around for car and renters insurance once a year.
Look at a cheaper prepaid phone plan. Many cost far less than the big carriers.
Cook at home more, and buy store brands for the basics.
And when your lease is up, think about a roommate or a cheaper place.

scenes.heading: Step 4: Make It Automatic
lines: The secret to sticking with it? Automate it.
On payday, move your twenty percent to savings before you can spend it.
Put your bills on autopay, so your needs are always covered.
Whatever is left in checking is your wants money. Spend it freely.

scenes.heading: 3 Mistakes to Avoid
lines: A few mistakes trip people up, so let's fix them now.
One: using your salary before taxes. Your numbers end up too big.
Two: calling every want a need. Be honest with yourself.
Three: forgetting costs that only come once or twice a year, like car repairs and gifts.
Divide those by twelve, and set that amount aside every month.

scenes.heading: Quick Recap
lines: Let's recap the whole plan in four steps.
Find your take-home pay.
Split it fifty, thirty, twenty.
Compare it with your real spending, and adjust if needs run high.
And automate your savings, so it happens without thinking.

scenes.heading: You've Got This
lines: You don't need a fancy app or a finance degree. Just three simple numbers.
If your twenty percent is starting from zero, watch our emergency fund video next.
If this helped, like the video and subscribe for a simple money tip every day.
Tell me in the comments: what are your three numbers? See you in the next one.
